slides.title: Fundamental Security Concepts Overview
defs: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability—the three foundational information-security objectives.
A security model that does not automatically trust users, devices, or connections.

slides.title: Confidentiality
slides.teach: Confidentiality means keeping information private from people who are not authorized to see it.

course.learn: Confidentiality means keeping information private from people who are not authorized to see it.

breakdown.explanation: Only approved people should be able to see sensitive information.
Encryption, passwords, MFA, access controls, and file permissions help protect confidentiality.

course.why: A confidentiality failure can expose passwords, personal information, financial records, or other sensitive data.
course.example: An employee emails a customer database containing Social Security numbers to the wrong person.
course.exam: If the scenario emphasizes unauthorized disclosure, exposure, reading, or viewing of data, think confidentiality.
course.check_q: A hacker reads unencrypted employee credentials while they travel across a network. Which CIA principle is affected?
course.check_a: Confidentiality, because someone who was not authorized was able to see the information.

slides.title: Integrity
slides.teach: Integrity means keeping information accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized changes.

course.learn: Integrity means keeping information accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized changes.

breakdown.explanation: You need to be able to trust that the data is still correct.
Hashing, digital signatures, checksums, permissions, and version controls can help protect integrity.

course.why: If data can be secretly altered, decisions made from that data may be wrong even if the system is still available.
course.example: An attacker changes employees' direct-deposit bank account numbers in a payroll system.
course.exam: If the scenario emphasizes modification, tampering, alteration, or whether data can be trusted, think integrity.
course.check_q: Malware modifies financial records without permission. Which CIA principle is affected?
course.check_a: Integrity, because the information was changed without authorization.

slides.title: Availability
slides.teach: Availability means making sure authorized users can access systems and information when they need them.

course.learn: Availability means making sure authorized users can access systems and information when they need them.

breakdown.explanation: The system or data needs to be usable when legitimate users need it.
Backups, redundancy, failover, load balancing, disaster recovery, and UPS systems can improve availability.

course.why: A secure system still fails its users if they cannot access it when it is needed.
course.example: A DDoS attack overwhelms an online store and legitimate customers cannot connect.
course.exam: If the scenario emphasizes downtime, outages, denial of service, or users being unable to access something, think availability.
course.check_q: A company's only database server fails and employees cannot access records. Which CIA principle is affected?
course.check_a: Availability, because authorized users cannot access the system when needed.

slides.title: Non-repudiation
slides.teach: Non-repudiation means providing proof that someone performed an action so they cannot reasonably deny doing it later.

course.learn: Non-repudiation means providing proof that someone performed an action so they cannot reasonably deny doing it later.

breakdown.explanation: You cannot say you did not do it when there is reliable evidence tying the action to you.
Digital signatures, audit logs, timestamps, and signed transactions can support non-repudiation.

course.why: Organizations may need evidence showing who approved, sent, signed, or performed an important action.
course.example: A manager digitally signs a financial transaction and later claims they never approved it.
course.exam: Look for phrases such as prove who performed the action, cannot deny, signed, or evidence of approval.
course.check_q: A company needs proof that a manager approved a transaction and cannot later deny the approval. Which concept applies?

slides.title: Authentication
slides.teach: Authentication means proving that you are who you claim to be.

course.learn: Authentication means proving that you are who you claim to be.

breakdown.explanation: Prove your identity.
Passwords, fingerprints, Face ID, smart cards, security tokens, and MFA are authentication methods.

course.why: Before a system decides what you are allowed to access, it first needs confidence in who you are.
course.example: A user enters a password and MFA code to sign in to a university account.
course.check_q: A user scans a fingerprint before signing in. Which AAA function is being performed?

slides.title: Authorization
slides.teach: Authorization means determining what an authenticated user is allowed to access or do.

course.learn: Authorization means determining what an authenticated user is allowed to access or do.

breakdown.explanation: Okay, I know who you are. Now what are you allowed to do?
File permissions, administrator privileges, role-based access, and read/write permissions are authorization decisions.

course.why: Two authenticated users can have very different permissions depending on their jobs or roles.
course.example: A student can view grades, while a professor can enter or modify grades.
course.exam: Authorization answers: What can you do? It normally comes after authentication.
course.check_q: A signed-in employee can read a file but cannot edit it. Which AAA function determines this?

slides.title: Accounting
slides.teach: Accounting means recording and tracking what users or systems do.

course.learn: Accounting means recording and tracking what users or systems do.

breakdown.explanation: Keep a record of their activity.
Login records, audit logs, session activity, file access logs, timestamps, and resource usage.

course.why: Accounting creates evidence that can support investigations, audits, troubleshooting, and accountability.
course.example: A log records when a user signed in, which files they opened, what they modified, and when they signed out.
course.exam: Accounting answers: What did you do?
course.check_q: A security system records every file an administrator accessed during a session. Which AAA function is this?

slides.title: Zero Trust
slides.teach: Zero Trust is a security approach where no user, device, or connection is automatically trusted, even if it is already inside the organization's network.

course.learn: Zero Trust is a security approach where no user, device, or connection is automatically trusted, even if it is already inside the organization's network.

breakdown.explanation: Being inside the network does not automatically make you trusted. Prove that you should have access.
Least privilege, MFA, device health checks, continuous evaluation, microsegmentation, and context-based access.

course.why: Attackers may already be inside a network, so trust should be based on verified identity, device condition, context, and need.
course.example: An employee successfully signs in, but each sensitive resource request is still evaluated before access is allowed.
course.exam: Remember: never trust automatically; always verify. Zero Trust also emphasizes least privilege and continuous evaluation.
course.check_q: A company requires identity and device checks before every sensitive application request, even for internal users. Which model is being used?

slides.title: Deception Technology
slides.teach: Deception technology uses fake resources to trick attackers into interacting with something that looks real.

course.learn: Deception technology uses fake resources to trick attackers into interacting with something that looks real.

breakdown.explanation: Give the attacker believable bait so defenders can detect or observe them.
Honeypots, honeynets, honeyfiles, and honeytokens are common deception technologies.

course.why: Legitimate users normally have no reason to interact with a decoy, so activity involving one can be a strong sign of suspicious behavior.
course.example: A fake server is intentionally made attractive to attackers so defenders can observe their actions.
course.exam: Deception means trick or bait. Know the difference between a honeypot, honeynet, honeyfile, and honeytoken.
course.check_q: A fake API key is planted in a repository and generates an alert if anyone uses it. What kind of deception resource is this?

slides.title: Disruption Technology
slides.teach: Disruption technology uses security techniques to interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow down an attack.

course.learn: Disruption technology uses security techniques to interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow down an attack.

breakdown.explanation: Do not just detect the attacker—interrupt what they are trying to accomplish.
Redirecting malicious traffic, sinkholing, isolating compromised systems, or sending attackers toward decoys can disrupt an attack.

course.why: Disruption can reduce an attacker's ability to communicate, move through the environment, or complete an attack.
course.example: Malware attempts to contact a malicious command-and-control server, but the traffic is redirected to a controlled sinkhole.
course.exam: Deception = trick the attacker. Disruption = interrupt the attacker.
course.check_q: Malware traffic is redirected away from its real command-and-control server to a controlled destination. Which concept is being used?

fundamental_concepts_layout.intro: This overview summarizes the fundamental security concepts you should recognize in Security+ scenarios. Focus on the simple meaning, the clue in the question, realistic examples, and the memory shortcuts.

overview.label: AAA
overview.question: Who are you, what can you do, and what did you do?

overview.label: Security Strategies & Assurance
overview.question: How do we manage trust, attackers, and proof?

cia.name: Confidentiality
cia.definition: Keeping information private from people who are not authorized to see it.
cia.exam_question: Was data exposed to someone who should not see it?
cia.scenario: An employee accidentally emails a customer database containing SSNs to the wrong person.

cia.name: Integrity
cia.definition: Keeping information accurate and protected from unauthorized changes.
cia.exam_question: Was data changed or tampered with?
cia.scenario: An attacker changes employees' direct-deposit bank account numbers in payroll.

cia.name: Availability
cia.definition: Making sure authorized users can access systems and data when needed.
cia.exam_question: Can authorized users access it when they need it?
cia.scenario: A DDoS attack overwhelms a website so legitimate customers cannot connect.

identity.name: Authentication
identity.definition: Proving that you are who you claim to be.

identity.name: Authorization
identity.definition: Determining what an authenticated user is allowed to access or do.

identity.name: Accounting
identity.definition: Recording and tracking what users or systems do.

aaa_rows: A user enters a password and MFA code.
A signed-in user can read a file but cannot edit it.
Logs record which files the user accessed and when.

strategies.name: Deception Technology
strategies.definition: Fake resources are intentionally created to trick attackers into interacting with something that looks real. The specific honey technologies are summarized in the detail chart below.

strategies.name: Disruption Technology
strategies.definition: Security techniques that interfere with, redirect, isolate, or slow down an attack.

strategies.name: Zero Trust
strategies.definition: No user, device, or connection is automatically trusted, even if it is already inside the organization's network.

strategies.name: Non-repudiation
strategies.definition: Providing proof that someone performed an action so they cannot reasonably deny doing it later.

deception_rows: Attracts attackers to a decoy machine or service so their behavior can be observed
Creates a decoy environment with multiple systems so attacker movement can be studied
Looks valuable and helps detect unauthorized access when someone opens or copies it
Triggers detection if fake credentials, API keys, accounts, or records are used

questions.q: A stolen laptop contains unencrypted customer records. Which CIA principle is MOST directly at risk?
questions.explanation: Confidentiality is concerned with preventing unauthorized disclosure of information.

questions.q: An attacker modifies product prices in an e-commerce database. Which CIA principle has been compromised?
questions.explanation: Integrity is affected because data was changed without authorization.

questions.q: A DDoS attack prevents customers from reaching a company's website. Which CIA principle is MOST affected?
questions.explanation: Availability is affected because legitimate users cannot access the service.

questions.q: A company needs to prove that a manager approved a financial transaction and prevent the manager from later denying the approval. Which concept BEST addresses this?
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation provides evidence that ties an action to a person so the action cannot reasonably be denied later.

questions.q: A user enters a password and an MFA code before being allowed to sign in. Which AAA function is being performed?
questions.explanation: Authentication verifies who the user is.

questions.q: After a user signs in, the system determines that the user may view reports but may not modify them. Which AAA function is this?
questions.explanation: Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to do.

questions.q: A system records the time a user logged in, which files were opened, and when the user logged out. Which AAA function is being performed?
questions.explanation: Accounting records and tracks user activity.

questions.q: An organization verifies identity, device health, and access context before allowing each sensitive request, even for users already on the internal network. Which model is this?
questions.explanation: Zero Trust does not automatically trust users or devices based on network location and continually evaluates access.

questions.q: A security team deploys a fake server that is intentionally attractive to attackers so their behavior can be observed. What is this?
questions.explanation: A honeypot is a decoy system designed to attract attackers.

questions.q: A fake API key is planted where an attacker may find it. Security is alerted if the key is ever used. What is this BEST described as?
questions.explanation: A honeytoken is fake data or a fake credential that should never be legitimately used.

questions.q: Malware attempts to contact a known command-and-control server, but the organization redirects the traffic to a controlled sinkhole. Which concept BEST describes this action?
questions.explanation: The organization is interfering with the attacker's communication, which is disruption.
